title: Run the without-text check the hard way
statement: Check that a question needs its new text the hard way: give the solver everything else the student has met, and judge by the worst of several option orders.
example: Re-run under four option orders and scored by the worst, 65 of 118 ordering items that had passed on one order were decertified.
detail: The reading courses' practice spec gives the solver all prior lesson content but not the new text; on one theme this caught 1 of 16 items that plain-blind certification missed (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/practice-layer-spec.md`, lines 106-109). The ordering gate had scored one seeded shuffle per item, and a re-probe of 118 certified ordering items under four shuffles, scored by the worst run beside a with-passage control, decertified 65 and flagged 7 as broken (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g5-reading/analysis/seq-reprobe-2026-07-07/README.md`). One item an older model solved 0/3 without the text, though 3/3 with the earlier lessons, was solved 3/3 without the text by a current model, so the old verdict did not survive model drift (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/handoffs-2026-07-13/course-eval-layer/README.md`, lines 86-92). Above all for items that ask for an order, try several option orders. Keep a with-text control beside the check, and repeat it whenever the solving model changes.
against: The prior-lessons check was measured on one theme, and the spec calls the result validation of the instrument on that bounded sample, not a general yield or course-readiness claim (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/practice-layer-spec.md`, lines 109-110). Elsewhere the same review counts a grade 5 decertification of 72 as 65 plus 7 broken-flagged items (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/course-red-team/SKILL.md`), so not all of the 72 may have been shuffle failures. A later run found: For items the platform serves in a fresh random order on every attempt, a Grade 5 course argued that the mean over resampled shuffles is a student's expected blind-solve performance and the worst case measures an attacker's luckiest presentation; judged by the mean, 31 ordering and 69 matching items the worst case had excluded were restored, none of the 31 solving exactly. The course's own retrospective lists assuming worst-case and mean-case were interchangeable as a failure, so which to judge by is open (`grade3-reading/_archive/2026-08-13-consolidation/dirty-state/ti-courseplans-untracked.tar.gz`). A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/_archive/2026-08-13-consolidation/dirty-state/ti-courseplans-untracked.tar.gz`).

Their expected blind-solve performance is therefore the **mean over resampled shuffles**, not the worst case. Worst-case measures an attacker's luckiest presentation, which no student controls under `shuffle="true"`.

- Restored (borderline under worst-case, safe under mean): 31 sequence + 69 match. **0 of the 31 restored sequences exact-solve; mean 0.31–0.58; worst 0.33–0.75.** The high worst-case values are lucky single-shuffle hits the student never reliably sees.

The sequence lane exposed a concrete protocol bug: a sequence item could pass if the blind solver saw only one seeded shuffle that happened not to reveal the ordering. A multi-shuffle reprobe decertified 65 items, flagged 7 broken items, and left 46 clean survivors.
